t: #3554 Find Category Recommendation Pairs — Category-Level Co-Purchase Counts
o: Like the product-pair problem but coarser: collapse each user's purchases to the set of categories, then count users sharing each unordered category pair. Users 1, 2, 5 share Books-Clothing → count 3, meeting the threshold. Deduplicate (user, category) first so multi-product baskets don't inflate counts, then self-join on user with category1 < category2.
k: Distinct (user, category) pairs are the atomic facts — build them once.
Self-join on user_id with a strict lexical inequality to canonicalize pairs.

a.i: Derive distinct user-category pairs in a subquery, join it to itself on user with ordering, group and filter.
s: Subquery: SELECT DISTINCT user_id, category from the join of purchases and info.
Self-join on user_id with a.category < b.category.
Group by the pair; HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) ≥ 3; order by count desc then names.

c.python:
SELECT a.category AS category1,
       b.category AS category2,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS customer_count
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT pp.user_id, pi.category
      FROM ProductPurchases pp
      JOIN ProductInfo pi ON pp.product_id = pi.product_id) a
JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT pp.user_id, pi.category
      FROM ProductPurchases pp
      JOIN ProductInfo pi ON pp.product_id = pi.product_id) b
  ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.category < b.category
GROUP BY a.category, b.category
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) >= 3
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, category1 ASC, category2 ASC;

a.i: Skip the subquery and join purchases to ProductInfo twice within one statement, relying on COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) to absorb multiplicity from multiple products per category.
s: Join ProductPurchases pa → ProductInfo a, and ProductPurchases pb (same user) → ProductInfo b with b.category > a.category.
Group by the category pair, HAVING on distinct users, order as required.

c.python:
SELECT a.category AS category1,
       b.category AS category2,
       COUNT(DISTINCT pa.user_id) AS customer_count
FROM ProductPurchases pa
JOIN ProductInfo a ON a.product_id = pa.product_id
JOIN ProductPurchases pb ON pb.user_id = pa.user_id
JOIN ProductInfo b ON b.product_id = pb.product_id AND b.category > a.category
GROUP BY a.category, b.category
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT pa.user_id) >= 3
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, category1 ASC, category2 ASC;

a.t: Join size driven by per-user basket products; DISTINCT count fixes correctness

w: The deduplicated-subquery version communicates intent best and avoids relying on DISTINCT aggregation to fix fan-out; the four-way join is shorter but leans on COUNT(DISTINCT). Strings compare lexicographically in SQL, so a.category < b.category implements category1 < category2 directly. Follow-up: exclude same-category pairs explicitly, or rank pairs within each category.
